strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: controllable, compositional generation of 3D anatomy for biophysical simulation is a genuinely useful capability, and the paper articulates design requirements (scale-critical control, attribute specificity, compositionality) that are specific to this domain rather than generic.

Simple, interpretable, and well-executed method: guiding an unconditional latent diffusion model with differentiable geometric moment losses (mass, centroid, scale-normalized covariance) requires no retraining, supports test-time composition of arbitrary numbers of components, and the presentation (Algorithm 1, Figure 2) is easy to follow.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation: the paper compares against three conditional-training baselines (explicit concatenation, implicit heatmap conditioning, cross-attention) with both conditional fidelity and generation-quality metrics (precision/recall, Fréchet distance, MMD, COV, 1-NNA), and includes ablations on disentangled losses (Table 1) and multi-component compositionality (Table 2).

End-to-end demonstration of value: the inpainting + biomechanical pressurization experiment (Figure 13) shows the framework can produce counterfactual anatomies usable in downstream FEM simulations, which grounds the claimed motivation.
Honest limitations section (weight tuning, unstable gradients for empty segmentations, topological artifacts) and a detailed appendix supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core method is a fairly straightforward application of loss-based diffusion guidance (DPS/universal guidance) with first- and second-order moments — a well-known family of techniques (self-guidance, universal guidance, composable diffusion are all cited). The composite loss and per-component application are sensible but incremental engineering rather than a new conceptual contribution.

Narrow empirical scope: all experiments are on a single dataset (596 manually filtered TotalSegmentator cardiac cases), a single architecture, and mostly a single constrained component (myocardium) for the main comparison. Generalization to other organs, datasets, or resolutions is untested, despite the paper framing this as a general anatomical framework.

Baseline fairness concerns: in Table 2, the implicit-conditioning baseline catastrophically fails at 0-1 components (FD of 1622/227 vs. 34.6/38.5 for the proposed method), which likely reflects a poorly configured dropout-conditioned baseline rather than a fundamental limitation of conditional approaches; the paper's interpretation that conditional models 'must be retrained' per component count is not convincingly established.

Hyperparameter fragility: the loss weights λ require per-loss experimental tuning with widely varying magnitudes (10^5-10^7), the temperature, softmax, guidance weight w, and ad hoc noise injection to stabilize empty-segmentation gradients all require manual intervention, which weakens the 'flexible, plug-and-play' claim.

Missing strong guidance baselines: comparisons to established inference-time guidance methods (e.g., universal guidance, DPS variants, manifold/attribute guidance adapted to moments) are absent; the only inference-time comparison is against the authors' own unconditional model.

No statistical uncertainty: results are based on 100-200 generated samples per setting without confidence intervals or significance tests, and several claimed differences (e.g., FD of 29.8 vs 32.7 in Table 2) look small.

Clinical/scientific validation is shallow: the simulation case study is a single patient with a synthetic 'toy' perturbation (doubling/halving RV mass) and an unvalidated neo-Hookean model; no expert evaluation, no comparison of simulated outcomes against known physiology, and no evidence the guided anatomies are physically plausible beyond aggregate distributional metrics.

strengths: The paper is clearly written with a well-motivated problem formulation (controllable, compositional generation of anatomical structures for biophysical simulation), and the method is easy to follow.

The evaluation is reasonably thorough: conditional fidelity, morphological distribution metrics (precision/recall, Fréchet distance), and pointcloud metrics (MMD, COV, 1-NNA) are used, with multiple conditional-training baselines (explicit, implicit, cross-attention) and ablations on loss terms and guidance weights.

The multi-component compositionality experiment (Table 2) demonstrates a genuine practical advantage over a dropout-trained conditional baseline, particularly at low component counts, and the downstream biomechanical inpainting example (Figure 13) shows a plausible end-use case.
The appendix provides substantial implementation detail (hyperparameters, weight tuning, dataset curation, simulation setup), supporting reproducibility.
Limitations are candidly discussed, including gradient instability for empty segmentations and topological artifacts.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core method is a fairly standard combination of well-established components: diffusion posterior sampling / universal guidance [50, 53] applied to differentiable moment-based losses (mass, centroid, covariance). Nothing here is conceptually new — the contribution is essentially an application and engineering of existing guidance techniques to cardiac label maps, which borders on domain-specific incremental work.

The claimed 'disentanglement' contribution is trivially achieved by zeroing out loss terms; since each loss is an additive term of a weighted sum, independent control follows almost by construction rather than from any learned disentangled representation. This framing overstates the contribution.

Evaluation scope is narrow. Quantitative comparisons in Sections 5.5-5.6 focus on a single component (myocardium or right ventricle) on a single dataset (596 curated cardiac segmentations). Generalization to other organs, datasets, or anatomies is not shown, which weakens the claim of a 'general inference-time framework'.

The guidance weights λi are tuned experimentally per loss (Table 5), and normalized moments with different scaling factors (10^4, 10^3) are reported, raising questions about how sensitive results are to these choices; no sensitivity analysis of the guidance weight w beyond a single sweep is provided.

Computational cost is not reported. Guidance requires decoding to voxel space and back-propagating through the VAE decoder at every denoising step, which is substantially more expensive than conditional sampling; the practical trade-off against conditional baselines (which appear competitive at 6 components in Table 2) is therefore unclear.

Baselines may be disadvantaged: the implicit baseline can only target mass indirectly through covariance (acknowledged in the appendix), and the explicit baseline cannot support unconditional sampling via dropout. A fairer comparison against other inference-time guidance methods (e.g., universal guidance with alternative loss formulations) is missing.

The demonstrated anatomical realism gains are modest: at higher component counts, the conditional baseline matches or exceeds the proposed method on most metrics (Table 2), so the main advantage is confined to the low-component regime.

Significance for a broad AI audience is limited; the work is most relevant to the medical imaging/simulation community, and the methodological contribution is unlikely to influence the wider generative modeling field.

Some technical fragility is admitted but not fully resolved (unstable gradients requiring ad hoc noise injection, topologically invalid outputs needing post-hoc filtering), which undercuts the paper's positioning for safety-critical simulation use.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: training-free, inference-time geometric guidance for 3D multi-component anatomical diffusion models addresses a genuine limitation of conditional-training approaches, which require retraining for every constraint configuration.

The moment-based decomposition (mass, centroid, scale-normalized covariance) maps directly to interpretable anatomical attributes (size, position, shape), and the weighted-sum formulation cleanly enables both disentangled attribute control and multi-component compositional constraints.

Evaluation is reasonably thorough: comparisons against three conditional-training baselines (explicit, implicit, cross-attention conditioning with CFG/ANG), sweeps over guidance weights, conditional fidelity plus distribution-level metrics (precision/recall, Fréchet distance, MMD, COV, 1-NNA), and ablations (Table 1) that specifically support the disentanglement claim.

The multi-component compositionality experiment (Table 2, Figures 10-11) provides concrete evidence that the method outperforms dropout-based conditional models when few components are constrained, which is the regime conditional models handle worst.

The downstream demonstration (mask-based inpainting + finite-element biventricular pressurization, Figure 13) connects the generative method to the motivating use case in biophysical simulation, strengthening significance beyond purely visual results.

Comprehensive appendix with hyperparameters, weight tuning, normalization constants, and simulation details supports reproducibility; limitations are discussed honestly (e.g., weight tuning, empty-segmentation gradient instability, topology errors).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially universal-guidance/DPS-style loss guidance [50, 51, 53] applied with standard geometric moments (mass, centroid, covariance). The 'key insight' that a linear combination of simple differentiable losses can jointly constrain generation is plausible but incremental; prior work (e.g., Kadry et al. [16]) already used loss-based morphological control, albeit with conditional training and size-only features.

Narrow empirical scope: a single anatomy type (cardiac) from a single dataset (596 curated TotalSegmentator segmentations). Generalization to other multi-component anatomies or domains is not demonstrated, weakening claims of a 'general inference-time framework'.
Main quantitative experiments (Figures 4-6, Table 1) constrain only the myocardium; breadth across the 10 labels is only shown qualitatively or in the compositional setting.

Mixed results are not fully acknowledged: in Table 2, the implicit conditioning baseline achieves better FD and comparable or better precision at 3 and 6 components, and in Figure 4 the method does not dominate all quality metrics; the narrative ('does not suffer in terms of generation quality') is somewhat stronger than the evidence.
No statistical significance testing or error bars over multiple runs/samplings; several reported differences (e.g., FD 29.8 vs 32.7) may be within sampling noise.

Guidance weights span several orders of magnitude (10^7 to 10^4) and are tuned experimentally per loss; sensitivity analysis to these weights and to the number of denoising steps is missing. The per-step VAE decode also implies significant inference-time cost, which is never quantified or compared against conditional sampling cost.

No comparison to alternative training-free guidance formulations (e.g., optimizing in latent space directly, other surrogate-loss designs, or topological regularization), so it is unclear the chosen moment losses are the best option for this task.

Missing comparison against other training-free approaches; the compositional baseline dropout experiment is constructed favorably (0-component implicit sampling necessarily degenerates), inflating the apparent gap at low component counts.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: controllable generation of anatomically realistic 3D label maps for biophysical simulation is a meaningful, underexplored application area, and the paper clearly articulates the fidelity-vs-control trade-off motivating inference-time guidance over conditional retraining.

Technically sound and clearly presented method: differentiable moment-based measurement functions (mass, centroid, scale-normalized covariance) are simple, interpretable, and well-suited to gradient guidance; the scale-normalized second moment enabling disentangled shape-vs-size control is a nice touch.

Unusually thorough and multi-faceted evaluation for a domain paper: sweeps over guidance weights, comparisons against three conditional-training baselines (explicit concatenation, implicit heatmaps, cross-attention with CFG/ANG), disentanglement ablations, multi-substructure compositionality (1/3/6 constraints), generality across four anatomical systems (cardiac, aorta, spine, knee), a toy ellipsoid study, dataset scaling analysis, VAE reconstruction lower-bound analysis, and editing-scale-factor analysis in the appendix.

Strong quantitative evidence that the proposed guidance improves conditional fidelity (Table 1, Figures 4 and 9) while maintaining distributional quality metrics (FD, precision/recall, MMD, coverage, 1-NNA), and that conditional dropout baselines fail under compositional constraints (Table 1, constraint count 0 and 1).

Practical end-to-end demonstration: guided inpainting for counterfactual RV editing followed by finite-element biomechanical simulation (Figure 11), plus an honest limitations section covering weight tuning, substructure granularity, and topological defects.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: energy-based guidance at inference time with differentiable losses is well established (universal guidance, DPS, diffusion self-guidance, compositional EBM samplers). The core contribution is applying moment-based losses to multi-class 3D segmentation latents; the method itself is a relatively straightforward instantiation of prior techniques in a new domain, which may limit impact beyond medical imaging.

Method requires nontrivial heuristics that weaken the 'no retraining/tuning' advantage: loss weights λ span 7 orders of magnitude and were tuned experimentally (Table 4); noise injection into mass denominators and guidance weight sweeps are needed for stability. The claim of generality rests on limited qualitative evidence for the three non-cardiac systems (no quantitative baselines there).

Guidance degrades topology: Table 8 shows geometric guidance increases Betti errors over unconditional sampling (e.g., Ao 1.208 → 1.458, IVC 0.125 → 0.417), which directly contradicts the paper's motivation that simulation-ready anatomy requires scale- and topology-critical fidelity; this issue is acknowledged but not solved or quantitatively bounded in the main results.

Small-scale evaluation: 596 cardiac training samples, 200 generated samples per comparison in the main conditional-fidelity study, 100 targets in compositionality/disentanglement experiments; some reported differences (e.g., Table 1 at 3 and 6 constraints) are small and no statistical significance or variance across seeds is reported.

Disentanglement claim has caveats: the observed mass-shape coupling is attributed to dataset correlation, and the evaluation of disentanglement (Figure 9) is confined to a single substructure (myocardium); conditional-fidelity metrics are computed against the very targets used for guidance, so no held-out verification of out-of-distribution constraint satisfaction is provided beyond the editing-scale sweep.

No discussion of inference-time compute cost relative to conditional baselines (guidance requires decoding to voxel space and differentiating through the VAE decoder every denoising step), and no public code or dataset release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well motivated: controllable generation of multi-class anatomical label maps for biophysical simulation is a legitimate and under-served application area, and the desiderata (scale-criticality, attribute specificity, compositionality, interpretability) are articulated well.

The proposed moment-based geometric losses (zeroth/first/second-order moments, with scale-normalized covariance) are simple, differentiable, and interpretable, and the ellipsoid visualization provides an intuitive interface for clinicians.

The experimental section is comparatively thorough for an application paper: it includes conditional-training baselines (explicit, implicit, cross-attention), guidance-weight sweeps, a disentanglement ablation, multi-substructure compositionality, generality across cardiac/aortic/spinal/knee datasets, a dataset-scaling analysis, a VAE-reconstruction and Betti-error analysis, and a downstream biomechanical simulation example.

The limitations section is honest, including the observation that geometric guidance increases Betti error for some structures, and the appendix addresses several potential confounds (e.g., noisy-mass stabilization).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The core technique is standard energy-based/universal guidance (Bansal et al., 2023; Chung et al., 2023) applied with MSE losses on geometric moments, which is a direct analogue of diffusion self-guidance (Epstein et al., 2023) in 3D label-map space. 'Compositional' control amounts to a weighted sum of per-substructure losses, which is the trivial composition of guidance terms, not a new mechanism. The contribution reads as an engineering application of existing guidance machinery rather than a new method.

Missing the most relevant baseline: the paper never compares against applying the same geometric moment losses via existing generic guidance frameworks (universal guidance, DPS, or manifold-preserving variants) that it cites. The only baselines are conditional-training approaches, so the reader cannot tell whether the proposed guidance formulation offers any advantage over simply plugging these losses into an off-the-shelf guidance scheme.

Weaknesses in the central 'disentanglement' claim. The shape-vs-size interaction is acknowledged (shape guidance improves mass fidelity), and targets are sampled from the validation distribution, so residual correlations in the data can leak into apparent disentanglement. A stronger evaluation would use out-of-distribution or adversarially constructed target combinations to show the losses are genuinely independent.

Evaluation is small-scale and lacks statistical rigor: 200 samples per method for the fidelity sweep, 100 for disentanglement/compositionality, on a modest 596-case cardiac dataset. No confidence intervals, no significance testing, and no repeated runs; several differences in Table 1 and Figure 4 (e.g., FD 32.7 vs 35.5, 1-NNA 0.52 vs 0.50) are likely within noise but are presented as evidence.

Baseline comparisons are not fully fair or fully informative. The '0 constraints' row of Table 1 shows the implicit baseline collapsing (FD 1622, precision 0.00), attributed to dropout imbalance, yet this degraded configuration frames the comparison; and the conditional baselines are trained with different guidance mechanisms (CFG vs ANG), making attribution unclear. The explicit-conditioning baseline reportedly cannot use dropout at all.

The most important application claim — that generated anatomy is suitable for biophysical simulation — rests on a single qualitative RV-editing example with three simulations. There is no quantitative evidence that guided samples are simulation-valid (e.g., mesh quality, physiologically plausible outputs across a cohort), and the paper's own Betti-error analysis shows guidance worsens topological defects for PA and IVC, which directly undermines simulation readiness.

Residual fidelity gaps are nontrivial: guided position and shape errors remain above the VAE reconstruction floor, and strong target scaling (factor 4) produces clearly distorted samples, meaning the method does not actually enforce constraints outside a narrow band around the data distribution — precisely where a controllable generator would be most useful (rare/pathological variants, per the introduction's motivation).

Loss weights (Table 4: 10^7, 10^5, 10^4) are hand-tuned with enormous spread, and no sensitivity analysis of these weights is provided in the main experiments, despite the authors acknowledging that the disentanglement behavior depends on them.

No code or data release is mentioned, and the multi-stage pipeline (specialized TotalSegmentator model, manual quality filtering, VAE + LDM training, in-house Fortran FEM solver) is difficult to reproduce from the appendix alone.

Some framing overstates the contribution: claims of 'advancing the state of the art' and 'unique' disentangled control are stronger than the evidence, given that conditional implicit heatmaps achieve comparable fidelity at 3-6 constrained substructures (Table 1), and prior work (Kadry et al., 2025; ProtComposer) already covers conditioned ellipsoid-based anatomical/protein generation.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: controllable generation of anatomically plausible 3D label maps is genuinely useful for in-silico trials, device design, and form-function studies, and the paper articulates the fidelity-vs-controllability trade-off well.

Technically sound framework: differentiable voxel-wise geometric moments (zeroth, first, and scale-normalized second order) are a clean, interpretable parameterization of substructure geometry, and the loss-based guidance (Eq. 3) is correctly formulated in analogy to diffusion posterior sampling.

Thorough evaluation relative to the field: the paper compares against three reasonable conditional-training baselines (explicit concatenation, implicit Gaussian heatmaps, cross-attention) and uses multiple metric families — conditional fidelity (L1 on moments), morphological distribution metrics (improved precision/recall, FMD), and pointcloud metrics (MMD, COV, 1-NNA with EMD).

The disentanglement ablation (Figures 5, 6, 9; Table 6) is convincing: individual losses improve their corresponding fidelity metric while leaving others largely unchanged, with an honest discussion of the size-shape correlation confound.

Strong generality section: the method is shown to transfer across cardiac, aortic, spinal, and knee datasets with the same loss weights, and to non-convex/branching substructures via Boolean unions of tissue classes.

Valuable downstream demonstration: the guided inpainting coupled to biventricular pressurization FEM simulations (Figure 11) connects the generative model to actual biophysical analysis, which is the point of the application domain.

Extensive appendix (dataset scaling, VAE reconstruction lower bound analysis, Betti error analysis, editing scale-factor sweep, alternative second-moment feature decomposition, procedural ellipsoid sanity check) increases confidence in the results and supports reproducibility.
Honest limitations section acknowledging loss-weight tuning, label-level substructure granularity, and topological defects.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core machinery is inference-time energy-based guidance with a differentiable loss, well established by universal guidance (Bansal et al. 2023), diffusion posterior sampling (Chung et al. 2023), and self-guidance (Epstein et al. 2023). The contribution is essentially a new loss family (geometric moments) applied to a new domain (3D multi-label anatomy), which is more of an application contribution than a methodological one.

Some head-to-head results are not clearly favorable: in Table 1 at 6 constrained substructures, the implicit conditioning baseline achieves better FD (31.1 vs 35.5) and MMD (8.11 vs 8.50), and the 0-substructure rows mostly demonstrate a dropout-configuration artifact of the baseline rather than an advantage of the proposed method. A more careful compositional baseline (e.g., energy-based composition of conditional models a la Du et al. 2023) would strengthen the claims.

Evaluation scale is modest: 200 samples for the main comparison and 100 for the ablations on a 596-case cardiac dataset; no confidence intervals or statistical tests are reported, and several claimed differences (e.g., in Figure 4 curves) are small.

Guidance weights (Table 4) span five orders of magnitude and are tuned experimentally; no sensitivity analysis of the weights is provided, leaving unclear how robust the approach is to new anatomies or new moment targets despite claims of transferability.

Topology degradation is acknowledged but not solved: Table 8 shows geometric guidance increases Betti errors relative to unconditional sampling (e.g., PA Betti error 0.583 -> 1.042), which directly undermines the stated goal of producing simulation-ready anatomy; no mitigation is evaluated.

Practical cost of guidance is not quantified: the method requires decoding to voxel space and backpropagating through the VAE decoder at every denoising step; inference-time and memory overhead versus conditional baselines is never reported.
The mass-denominator instability is patched with an ad-hoc noise injection (Section 8.4.1) rather than a principled fix, and its effect on gradient quality is not analyzed.

Realism claims would be strengthened by downstream validation beyond one simulation example (single patient, single scenario); the form-function causal claim in the conclusion rests on a single demonstration.
